chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Captives were brought to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), and a man from them was presented to have his neck struck. So Jibra'il said to him: 'Delay this one for today, O Muhammad.' So he returned him and brought out another, until he was the last of them. So he called for him to have his neck struck, but Jibra'il said to him: 'O Muhammad, your Lord conveys greetings to you and says to you: This captive of yours feeds food, entertains guests, is patient in adversity, and carries burdens.'

The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said to him: 'Jibra'il has informed me about you from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with such and such.' And I have hereby emancipated you.' He said to him: 'Does your Lord love this?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'I testify that there is no god but Allah, and you are the Messenger of Allah, and by the One who sent you with the truth as a prophet, I shall not repel anyone from my wealth, ever!'

key_terms.لَا رَدَدْتُ عَنْ مَالِي أَحَداً: I did not turn anyone away from my wealth

ai.seo_question: What virtues of a captive led to his emancipation according to the Prophet's experience with Jibra'il?
ai.summary: In this narrative from *Al-Kafi*, the Angel Jibra'il acts as a divine intermediary, revealing the captive's hidden virtues—specifically hospitality and endurance—to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), leading to his emancipation. This incident underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on *ihsan* (excellence in conduct) and *karam* (generosity) as tangible criteria for divine favor, illustrating how social virtues can directly influence spiritual status and historical events.
